column4: God sends water down, conducts it into springs within the earth, and brings out varied crops; this directly joins supplied water, hidden storage, and controlled release.

Rain makes valleys flow according to their measure, each carrying what fits it; measured reception by distinct vessels is a close natural parallel to souls and communities receiving apportioned contents.

Within Salih's address, Thamud are reminded that they dwell among gardens and springs; the disputed camel-turn therefore belongs to an explicitly water-rich setting whose abundance still has a binding order.

God guided Thamud, but they preferred blindness to guidance and were seized by a humiliating blast for what they earned; moral disclosure, chosen fujur, and the people's earned consequence meet in one retelling.
God reveals a spirit from His command to the Prophet, who had not known scripture or faith, and makes it a guiding light; this precisely depicts God-given inward disclosure producing guidance.
When revelation descends, it increases believers in faith and they rejoice, showing divine speech entering recipients and augmenting one moral orientation.
Moses' mother's heart becomes empty and God strengthens it so that she remains among the believers; this is a concrete divine intervention in the same inward recipient who was inspired to nurse him.
God had prevented Moses from accepting other nursing women, making his reception of milk selective and preparing the restoration of the inspired mother-child bond.
God returns Moses to his mother so that she may be comforted and know His promise is true; the nursing episode becomes the embodied fulfillment of the inspiration she received.
The righteous drink from a cup blended with camphor, presenting an assigned drink as the concrete form of their moral outcome.
God's servants drink from a spring that they cause to gush abundantly, closely matching the source dictionary's sense of a drink made available for its recipient to take freely.
People acknowledge their sins after mixing a righteous deed with another evil deed; both opposed moral contents are present in one human case, closely paralleling the soul's fujur and taqwa.
Every soul finds both the good and the evil it did brought before it, joining the two moral poles to the individual soul and its received consequence.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good sees it, making even the smallest positive moral portion perceptible and fully returned.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil sees it, completing the exact two-sided measure of moral consequence.
The command to give full measure and weight with justice is paired with the rule that no soul is burdened beyond capacity; fair shares, exact measure, and the individual soul converge explicitly.
Shuayb orders his people to give full measure and weight and not diminish what belongs to others, a direct ethical parallel to honoring another recipient's allotted share.
Shuayb again commands full measure and just weight and forbids depriving people of their things, restating the structure violated when a group preserves its access while denying the camel's.
The command to give full measure and not be among those who cause loss directly opposes taking one's own complete portion while diminishing another's.
The next command requires weighing with a straight balance, adding impartial measurement to the passage's demand for full shares.
The people are forbidden to diminish others' things, completing the passage's concrete parallel to violating a divinely assigned entitlement.
The believers are told to cooperate in righteousness and taqwa but not in sin and aggression, an enacted social separation of the two moral directions disclosed within the soul.
Had the towns believed and practiced taqwa, blessings from sky and earth would have opened; denial instead brings seizure, linking moral response to whether provision or punishment is received.

Salih asks his people why they seek to hasten evil before good and urges them to seek forgiveness; it matches their challenge to bring punishment after violating the camel warning and names the two outcomes they choose between.
God tells Job to strike the ground and identifies the resulting water as a cool washing place and drink, a personally assigned drink brought forth by direct divine provision.

The same descending revelation adds impurity to those whose hearts are diseased, contrasting with its increase of faith in 9:124 and showing one divine input received according to opposed inward states.
God saves those who believed and practiced taqwa from Thamud's blast, marking the boundary between the two moral receptions and their different shares of the outcome.
A garden's water may sink so deep that its owner cannot seek it, another concrete limit on the human assumption that an available water-share remains under personal control.
When the command comes, God saves Salih and the believers by mercy while disgrace takes the violators, separating the shares of the messenger's two audiences.
God sends winds before mercy and pure water from the sky; this ayah supplies the source and purity of the water used to revive land and water creatures in 25:49.
God pours water down abundantly, beginning a sequence that ends by naming the resulting growth as provision for humans and livestock.
God splits the earth open after pouring the water, showing the drink-bearing provision entering and opening its receiving ground before growth appears.
Fruit and pasture are among what the watered, split earth produces, adding the grazing side of the camel's drink-and-pasture scene.
The entire water-and-growth sequence is called provision for people and their livestock, uniting both classes of recipients under one divine supply.
The water and pasture brought out in 79:31 are identified as provision for people and their livestock, completing the shared sustenance scene.
Human progeny is made from an extract of humble fluid, preparing the fashioned, inwardly equipped human of 32:9 and reinforcing the living self's dependence on water-like substance.
The human was a drop of emitted fluid before being created and proportioned in 75:38, supplying the liquid origin immediately before the act of making fit.
Thamud are destroyed by the overwhelming calamity, another concise retelling of the particular people's received consequence after the camel episode.
God sends Salih to Thamud to worship Him, but the people split into contending factions; it identifies the same messenger and the divided moral audience addressed by the camel warning.
God directs attention to the outcome of the plot against Salih: He destroys the plotters and all their people, repeating the communal consequence attached to rejection of this messenger.
God saves those who believed and practiced taqwa from that destruction, preserving the taqwa-side of the moral division within the Salih narrative.
Immediately after wrongdoers are assigned their portion, woe is pronounced for them on their promised day; this identifies the temporal destination of the share in 51:59.
God opens a person's chest to submission and gives light from Him, while hardened hearts stand in manifest error; opposed inward capacities clarify how divine guidance can be received.
God's message makes skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften to His remembrance, giving bodily form to revelation entering and transforming its recipients.
The command to give full measure and weigh with a straight balance repeats the requirement that apportioned rights be honored accurately.
People must establish weight with justice and not make the balance deficient, a general boundary against reducing another's measured due.
The arrogant chiefs ask the believers whether they know Salih is sent by his Lord, keeping the messenger's authority under explicit debate between the camel warning and its violation.
The arrogant reply that they disbelieve in Salih's message, supplying the inward stance that immediately issues in hamstringing the camel.
God asks no provision from creatures and does not ask them to feed Him; before He names Himself the Provider, the giver-recipient relation is decisively reversed away from God as a needy consumer.
Believers are asked whether the time has come for their hearts to humble to God's remembrance and revealed truth, presenting the heart's proper reception of what descends from Him.
Those given knowledge recognize the revelation as truth, believe in it, and have their hearts submit humbly, a specific sequence from divine communication to inward reception.
